Mutter
MUT-er
v. (to murmur indistinctly; to speak in a low voice)
Hebrew hagah, to murmur, to growl, to utter a low sound — the same verb rendered meditate at Psalm 1:2. What distinguishes the two uses is not the sound but the source: the muttering of the medium is set against meditation on the law.

Biblical Definition

And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead? Isaiah is describing the ordinary traffic of a nation that has lost confidence in the word of God, and he describes it with contempt for the sound of it. The mediums peep and mutter — chirping and murmuring, the theatrical half-audible voices of the trade. The prophet's reply is two rhetorical questions that dismantle the whole enterprise. Should not a people seek unto their God? — they have a God who speaks plainly and they are consulting substitutes. And for the living to the dead? — the direction of the inquiry is absurd, the living seeking guidance from the dead. Then Isaiah gives the test that settles every such claim, and it is the standing biblical rule for assessing any word purporting to come from God: to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. The law had long since closed the door on the practice altogether — regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them — and Deuteronomy lists the consulter with familiar spirits, the wizard, and the necromancer among the abominations for which the nations were driven out.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): to utter words with a low voice and compressed lips, with sullenness or in complaint; to murmur; to grumble.

expand to see more

MUTTER, v.i. To utter words with a low voice and compressed lips, with sullenness or in complaint; to grumble; to murmur.

MUTTER, v.t. To utter with imperfect articulations, or with a low voice.

MUTTERING, ppr. Uttering with a low voice; murmuring.

WIZARD, n. A conjurer; an enchanter; a sorcerer.

NECROMANCY, n. The art of revealing future events by means of a pretended communication with the dead.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 8:19 — "And when they shall say unto you, Seek unto them that have familiar spirits, and unto wizards that peep, and that mutter: should not a people seek unto their God? for the living to the dead?"

Isaiah 8:20 — "To the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them."

Leviticus 19:31 — "Regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them: I am the LORD your God."

Deuteronomy 18:11 — "Or a charmer, or a consulter with familiar spirits, or a wizard, or a necromancer."

Modern Corruption

Divination is treated as harmless entertainment or as a spiritual practice compatible with faith; Scripture names it as defilement and supplies a plain test for every claimed word from God.

expand to see more

Consulting the dead and the spirits has never gone away; it has been rebranded. Mediums, psychics, horoscopes, tarot, and the apps that deliver them are the same trade Isaiah describes, and the fact that most participants regard it as amusement changes the practice not at all. Leviticus does not grade it by the sincerity of the enquirer: regard not them that have familiar spirits, neither seek after wizards, to be defiled by them. The defilement attaches to the seeking. And the question Isaiah asks is the one that exposes the absurdity to anyone who has a Bible: a people who possess the speech of the living God are going elsewhere to be muttered at.

Isaiah 8:20 also supplies the test the church needs against a nearer error, since not every claimed revelation comes from a medium. The New Apostolic Reformation and the wider prophetic movement produce a steady stream of words said to be from the Lord, and the biblical rule applies without modification: to the law and to the testimony: if they speak not according to this word, it is because there is no light in them. The dictionary holds the closed canon and the cessation of the revelatory gifts, and notes that the test Isaiah gives would be sufficient even for those who do not: a word that cannot be checked against Scripture is not to be received, whatever voice delivers it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew hagah (H1897), to murmur or mutter; ob (H178), a familiar spirit; yiddeoni (H3049), a wizard or knowing one; tsaphaph (H6850), to chirp or peep.

expand to see more

Hebrew hagah (H1897) — to murmur, to growl; rendered mutter here and meditate at Psalm 1:2.

Hebrew ob (H178) — a familiar spirit, or the medium who has one; the word used of the witch of Endor.

Hebrew yiddeoni (H3049) — a knowing one, a wizard; always paired with ob in the prohibitions.

Hebrew tsaphaph (H6850) — to chirp as a bird; rendered peep, of the medium's voice.

Hebrew torah (H8451) — law, instruction; the first half of the test at Isaiah 8:20.

Usage

"“wizards that peep, and that mutter” — the theatrical voices of the trade."

"“for the living to the dead?” — the absurdity of the direction."

"“to the law and to the testimony” — the test for every claimed word."
